lead: This unit explains how a beam carries transverse load through bending and shear stresses. You will find section properties, apply the bending equation, compute stress distributions and section modulus, handle flitched beams, analyse shear stress and shear centre, and size a beam for both flexure and shear. After it you can calculate safe loads, choose a section, and check a design against allowable stresses.
about: Unit 4 begins with 4.1, where you find the centroid and second moment of area of a section. These give the neutral axis and I used in 4.2, the theory of simple bending and the equation M/I = σ/y = E/R. Chapter 4.3 turns the equation into a stress diagram and defines section modulus, so you can get load capacity. Chapter 4.4 extends the idea to flitched beams of timber and steel. Chapter 4.5 derives shear stress and shear flow across common sections, and 4.6 explains shear centre, the point that avoids twisting. Chapter 4.7 uses both bending and shear checks to size a beam. Each chapter uses the earlier one, so work in order.

chapters.idea: A section's centroid and second moment of area fix where the neutral axis lies and how stiff the section is in bending.
chapters.depth: Centroid of composite areas by first moments; second moment of area (moment of inertia) about centroidal axes; parallel-axis theorem I = I_c + A d²; perpendicular-axis theorem for axes in the plane; I for rectangle, circle, triangle, I- and T-sections. Some syllabi call second moment of area moment of inertia. Keep integration to standard shapes only.

figure.title: I by parts
figure.aria: Flowchart: split a section into rectangles, find each area and centroid, locate the overall centroid, apply the parallel-axis theorem, and sum to get the second moment of area about the neutral axis.

chapters.example: A T-section has a flange 120 mm wide and 20 mm deep and a web 20 mm thick and 80 mm deep, total depth 100 mm. Find the centroid from the bottom and the second moment of area about the horizontal centroidal axis. Answer: ȳ = 70 mm from bottom; I = 3.333 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
chapters.trap: Taking the centroid from the top when dimensions are given from the bottom, and adding A d² with d measured to the wrong axis. For a T-section the centroid is not at mid-depth.
chapters.leave: Bending stress to 4.2; shear stress to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Plane sections and Hooke's law turn a bending moment into a linear stress field through M/I = σ/y = E/R.
chapters.depth: Pure bending; assumptions: plane sections stay plane, homogeneous isotropic material, Hooke's law, small deflection, constant E, no shear. Derivation from strain ε = y/R to stress σ = E y/R and moment equilibrium; bending equation M/I = σ/y = E/R. Define M (bending moment), I (second moment about neutral axis), σ (bending stress), y (distance from neutral axis), E (Young's modulus), R (radius of curvature). Sign convention. Limitations where shear is large.

figure.title: Bending equation path
figure.aria: Flowchart: plane sections give strain proportional to distance from the neutral axis, Hooke's law gives stress, moment equilibrium gives the bending equation.

chapters.example: A rectangular beam 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep carries a bending moment of 5 kN·m. Take E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum bending stress and the radius of curvature. Answer: I = 4.167 × 10⁶ mm⁴; σ = 60 MPa; R = 167 m.
chapters.trap: Putting kN·m straight into the formula with mm and N/mm²; convert to N·mm. Measure y from the neutral axis, not from the top, unless the section is symmetric and you know the axis.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for I and neutral axis; Unit 3 for bending moment.
chapters.leave: Shear stress to 4.5, deflection to Unit 5, design to 4.7.

chapters.idea: Bending stress is largest at the farthest fibre, so section modulus Z = I/y_max gives the moment capacity M = σ Z.
chapters.depth: Linear stress distribution σ = M y/I; maximum stress at the farthest fibre; section modulus Z = I/y_max and M = σ Z; moment of resistance; Z for rectangle bd²/6, circle πd³/32, I- and T-sections from I/y_max; stress diagrams for symmetric and unsymmetric sections; load carrying capacity and proportioning of sections. Some syllabi call Z the modulus of section.

figure.aria: Plot of bending stress against distance from the neutral axis for a 200 mm deep beam at 10 MPa extreme fibre stress; the line passes through zero at the neutral axis and is maximum at the top and bottom fibres.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam of span 3 m carries a central point load W. Its rectangular section is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep, and the allowable bending stress is 10 MPa. Find the safe load W. Answer: Z = 666,667 mm³; M = 6.667 kN·m; W = 8.89 kN.
chapters.trap: Using total depth/2 as y_max for an unsymmetric section; y_max is the distance from the neutral axis to the farthest fibre. Also do not use bd²/6 for bending about the weak axis without swapping b and d.
chapters.leave: Flitched beams to 4.4; shear design to 4.7; deflection to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Two materials bolted together share a bending moment in proportion to their stiffness, handled by a modular ratio and a transformed section.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Flitched or composite beams of timber and steel plates bolted together; plane sections and same curvature; modular ratio m = E_steel/E_timber; transformed section; stress in steel = m times stress in timber at the same y; moment shared in proportion to EI; simple stress check. Keep to two materials and full composite action.

figure.aria: Stack diagram of a flitched beam section: a timber core with a steel plate on top and a steel plate on the bottom.

chapters.example: A flitched beam has a timber core 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep and two steel plates 100 mm wide and 10 mm thick, one on top and one on bottom. Take E_steel = 200 GPa and E_timber = 10 GPa. For a bending moment of 30 kN·m, find the maximum stress in timber and in steel. Answer: m = 20; I_transformed = 5.08 × 10⁸ mm⁴; σ_timber = 5.91 MPa; σ_steel = 124 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using the actual steel width in the transformed section instead of m times the width, or forgetting to multiply the stress by m when reporting steel stress. Full composite action needs connectors; do not assume it silently.
chapters.leave: Shear connector design and shear stress distribution to 4.5 and 4.7; torsion to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Shear force creates a parabolic shear stress across a section, found from τ = VQ/(Ib) and shear flow q = VQ/I.
chapters.depth: Shear stress formula τ = VQ/(I b); Q is first moment of the area beyond the level, b is width at that level; shear flow q = VQ/I. Distribution for rectangle (τ_max = 1.5 V/A), circle (4/3 V/A), triangle, I- and T-sections (web carries most shear). Zero shear stress at free surfaces; maximum at neutral axis for rectangle. Some syllabi call this horizontal shear stress.

figure.aria: Plot of shear stress against distance from the neutral axis for a 200 mm deep rectangular beam; the distribution is parabolic, zero at the top and bottom fibres and maximum at the neutral axis.

chapters.example: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a shear force of 60 kN. Find the maximum shear stress and the shear stress at 50 mm from the neutral axis. Answer: I = 66.667 × 10⁶ mm⁴; τ_max = 4.5 MPa; at y = 50 mm, τ = 3.375 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using average shear V/A as the maximum; for a rectangle τ_max = 1.5 V/A. In an I-section take b as the web thickness at the level where you want τ, and take Q for the area above or below that level.
chapters.leave: Shear centre to 4.6; design to 4.7; torsion shear to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The shear centre is the load point that produces no twisting of a beam section.
chapters.depth: Shear centre (flexural centre): point through which a transverse load gives no twist. Symmetric sections: on the axis of symmetry; doubly symmetric: at centroid. Thin-walled open sections: shear flow in flanges creates a torque that is balanced by an offset e. Channel formula e = b²/(2b + h/3) for thin walls, where b is flange width and h is web depth. Concept of shear flow; unsymmetrical bending avoided.

figure.title: Shear centre idea
figure.aria: Flowchart: an off-centre load twists the section; shear flow in the flanges creates a balancing torque at an offset e, so a load through the shear centre causes no twist.

chapters.example: A thin-walled channel has web depth h = 200 mm and flange width b = 100 mm, with uniform thickness t. Find the shear centre distance from the web centreline. Answer: e = b²/(2b + h/3) = 37.5 mm from the web centreline, outside the web.
chapters.trap: Treating shear centre as the centroid. For a channel the centroid is inside the web, but the shear centre lies outside it. A load through the centroid still causes twist.
chapters.leave: Full thin-walled unsymmetric shear flow to advanced study; design to 4.7.

chapters.idea: A beam is safe when its section modulus meets the bending stress limit and its shear area meets the shear stress limit.
chapters.depth: Working stress design: maximum bending moment from BMD; required Z = M/σ_allow; choose a standard or rectangular section; check τ_max = 1.5 V/A for rectangle or VQ/(Ib) generally; proportioning for balanced bending and shear; beams of uniform strength (concept). Some syllabi call this design of beam for flexure and shear. Do not include limit-state factors.

figure.title: Design checks
figure.aria: Flowchart: find the maximum bending moment, get the required section modulus, choose a section, check shear stress, and accept the final size.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries a uniform load of 20 kN/m. Allowable bending stress is 160 MPa and allowable shear stress is 100 MPa. Design a rectangular section with depth twice width and check shear. Answer: M = 40 kN·m; Z_req = 250,000 mm³; b ≈ 72 mm, d ≈ 144 mm; choose 75 mm × 150 mm; τ_max = 5.33 MPa < 100 MPa.
chapters.trap: Designing for bending only and not checking shear; or using V/A instead of 1.5V/A for a rectangle. Keep M in N·mm and stress in N/mm² so Z comes in mm³.
chapters.leave: Deflection checks to Unit 5; torsion to Unit 6; columns to Unit 7.
